data.name: RTB101
data.description: An oral ATP-competitive inhibitor of both class I PI3K and mTOR (dactolisib, formerly BEZ235), used at low doses intended to hit TORC1; tested for immune function in older adults, where it raised antiviral gene expression but failed its phase 3 clinical endpoint.
data.description_beginner: An oral drug that blocks both class I PI3K and mTOR (also called dactolisib, formerly BEZ235), given at low doses meant to hit mTORC1 rather than everything at once. It was tested for boosting immune function in older adults: it raised antiviral gene activity in early trials but failed to meet its goal in a larger, phase 3 clinical trial.

studies.title: TORC1 inhibition enhances immune function and reduces infections in the elderly
studies.authors: Mannick JB; Morris M; Hockey HP; Roma G; Beibel M; Kulmatycki K; Watkins M; Shavlakadze T; Zhou W; Quinn D; Glass DJ; Klickstein LB

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: A phase 2a RCT in 264 older adults: 6 weeks of a low-dose combination of BEZ235 (a catalytic PI3K/mTOR inhibitor) and everolimus (RAD001) was associated with fewer reported infections over the following year, plus higher antiviral gene expression and a better flu-vaccine response. The later phase 3 trial of RTB101 (BEZ235) alone (MAN2021) did not confirm a clinical benefit.

studies.title: Targeting the biology of ageing with mTOR inhibitors to improve immune function in older adults: phase 2b and phase 3 randomised trials
studies.authors: Mannick JB; Teo G; Bernardo P; Quinn D; Russell K; Klickstein L; Marshall W; Shergill S

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: This paper reports two trials of RTB101, a drug that blocks mTOR, taken once a day for 16 weeks by adults over 65. In the phase 2b trial (652 people), fewer people on 10 mg had a lab-confirmed respiratory infection than on placebo (19% against 28%), but that result comes from a pooled analysis the authors did not correct for multiple testing, and the corrected analysis did not reach significance. The phase 3 trial (1,024 people) used a different main endpoint, set with the FDA: symptoms with or without a lab test. It found no difference (26% against 25%, p = 0.65), although blood tests still showed more antiviral genes switched on in both trials. In phase 2b, twice-daily dosing and a combination with everolimus did not reach significance, which the authors read as a hint that on-off inhibition may beat constant inhibition. Those numbers are "data not shown" in the paper. Boundary: RTB101 is not rapamycin or everolimus, the phase 3 group was healthier (no COPD, no smokers), and that trial was too small to test the lab-confirmed endpoint. The only everolimus arm (RTB101 plus everolimus 0.1 mg daily) was a combination and did not reach significance, which is why this paper is listed against the everolimus and immune function link on the pathway map. It cannot show what everolimus alone does.
